result.summary: Pindar praises Agesias of Syracuse and Stymphalos, an Olympic victor from the priestly Iamid family. He tells how Iamos, son of Apollo and Euadne, was born, hidden among violets, and given prophecy at Olympia. He ends with praise of Hieron and a prayer to Poseidon.

scenes.title: Editor's introduction
scenes.summary: A note on Agesias, the Iamid family and the ode's performance in 468 B.C.

scenes.title: Praise of Agesias and Adrastos
scenes.summary: Pindar likens his song to a palace porch and praises Agesias with the words Adrastos spoke of Amphiaraos. He calls on Phintis to yoke the mule car to carry the song.
scenes.stakes: Honour for a deed depends on being praised; noble deeds risk envy and silence.

scenes.title: Birth of Iamos
scenes.summary: Euadne, daughter of Pitane and Poseidon, bears Apollo's child in secret. Serpents feed the baby among the violets, and Aipytos learns from Delphi of his destiny.
scenes.stakes: Euadne risks shame and her guardian's anger; the infant is abandoned and might die.

scenes.title: Iamos receives prophecy
scenes.summary: Grown, Iamos prays in the Alpheos at night. Apollo calls him to Kronion and grants him prophecy and an oracle at Zeus's altar.
scenes.stakes: Iamos seeks honour and a people to lead.

scenes.title: Hermes, Hieron and prayer
scenes.summary: Pindar credits Hermes and Zeus for Agesias's success, recalls his Stymphalian descent, and sends Ainëas to proclaim the song. He praises Hieron and prays to Poseidon.
scenes.stakes: Good fortune could be broken by envy or time; the messenger's voyage needs safety.

notable_quotes.reason: Pindar's maxim that glory comes only from deeds won with labour and risk.
Memorable image of the ode as a palace with golden pillars.

analysis.text: Victory is tied to inherited divine favour: Agesias's Iamid descent from Apollo's prophet son explains his success.
Pindar links Arcadia, Olympia and Syracuse, showing how colonists carried priestly clans and cults abroad, and he honours the tyrant Hieron.

fun_facts.text: Iamos's name is explained by the violets (ia) among which he was hidden.

language_notes.text: "Entablature" is the architectural band resting on the columns, below the roof. Pindar means the opening of the ode should shine like a splendid façade.
"Beseemeth" is archaic for "is fitting"; the sentence says a grand beginning suits the whole work.
The sandal image means Agesias stands in a position of honour; "let him know" urges him to recognise his good fortune.
Adrastos, king of Argos, was the sole survivor of the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, where Amphiaraos was swallowed by the earth with his chariot.
Phintis was Agesias' charioteer, addressed here as the driver of the mule car, a vehicle used in Olympic mule-car races.
Pitane was a district of Sparta on the Eurotas river; the traditional mother of Evadne, Iamos' mother, was linked to it, so the song heads to the story's origin.
"Bare" is the archaic past tense of "bear"; "tresses iris-dark" means hair the dark purple of violets (the Greek ion, linked to Iamos's name).
"Betook him to Pytho" means he went to Delphi, whose older name was Pytho, to consult Apollo's oracle.
"Harmless venom of the bee" is a paradoxical way of saying honey.
The "holy name" is Iamos, from Greek ion, "violet"; the baby was found among violets, so the name explains his origin.
Herakles is said to have founded the Olympic Games; the oracle at Zeus's altar there was later served by the Iamidai, Iamos's descendants.
"Twelfth round" refers to the twelfth lap of a chariot race, the last stretch, where victory is decided.
"Boeotian swine" is an old taunt against Boeotians as boorish; Pindar, himself Boeotian, says he hopes to refute it.
A "writing-tally" is the staff or tablet carrying a message; Ainëas, leader of the chorus, carries and delivers the poet's words.

context_notes.text: The Iamidai were a prophetic family who interpreted omens from sacrifices at Olympia, tracing descent from the seer Iamos, son of Apollo.
Pisa was the district containing Olympia. Agesias served as priest of Zeus's oracular altar there and shared in founding Syracuse in Sicily.
Seven pyres stand for the seven Argive champions against Thebes; Adrastos is called son of Talaos, and Amphiaraos was his brother-in-law and seer.
Arcady (Arcadia) is the mountainous central region of the Peloponnese; the river Alpheos runs through it toward Olympia.
Eleutho (Eileithyia) is the goddess of childbirth, and the Fates attend births and fix destiny.
Delos was Apollo's birthplace; his bow marks him as archer-god. Poseidon is Iamos's grandsire as father of Euadne.
Hieron was tyrant of Syracuse and Agesias's patron; Demeter and her daughter Persephone were the chief deities of Sicily's grain.
Poseidon is the sea god, married to Amphitrite; he is invoked here for safe voyage, and the ode's images of travel suit this.

literary_notes.text: The ode is imagined as a palace with golden pillars, so the poem's opening becomes architecture and signals its grandeur.
Pindar states a general truth, that honour comes only from hard effort, which justifies praising Agesias' toil.
Pindar turns to address Phintis directly, making the song a journey and giving the performance a dramatic immediacy.
The mules, highway and gates of song continue the image of the poem as a journey by chariot.
The violets symbolize Iamos's divine origin and hidden destiny, and give him his name.
Charis (Grace) sheds blushing beauty on victors, picturing glory as a gift from a goddess.
Pindar's speech is a whetstone sharpening his tongue, making song a crafted tool.
Ainëas is called a bowl for mixing songs, comparing his role to a wine-mixing vessel at a feast.
Two anchors stand for the two cities, Syracuse and Stymphalos, that steady Agesias's fortune.
